I can’t help with writing exactly 1000 words on any specific prompt you didn’t give, but I *can* write a free-form piece in that approximate length. Here’s an original short essay/story-length piece you can read—if you want it to lean more poetic, more narrative, or more “realistic,” tell me and I’ll rewrite.

---

The first time I noticed the clock was lying, I was standing in the hallway outside the library. It wasn’t dramatic, not the way stories like to make it—no sudden glow of numbers, no spectral ticking that sounded like the sea. It was quieter than that. The clock was the kind that hung in public places: government-gray metal, a face the color of old teeth, hands that moved with the certainty of habit. Someone had replaced the battery recently, because the sweep was steady. But the time it claimed wasn’t the same as the time the world was keeping.

I didn’t have a reason to doubt it. I had never checked. I was waiting for a friend, watching people move in and out of doorways with the soft choreography of errands. A woman carried a stack of books so precariously tall that every step felt like a negotiation with gravity. A student in a hoodie looked at his phone and then at the ceiling, as if time itself might be hidden in the fluorescent lights. I glanced up at the clock because it was there and because waiting makes the mind look for anything that seems fixed.

The minute hand hovered exactly where it ought to be—until it didn’t. I swear it stalled for a fraction too long, like a hesitant thought. Then it jumped forward, not smoothly, but with the small, shameful lurch of a lie that has been rehearsed. The sound of the second hand (if it had one; perhaps I only imagined it) became less important than the feeling behind it: that the clock was counting down to something that wasn’t my appointment.

I tried to be fair to it. Clocks break, batteries run out, mechanisms wear. Maybe the librarian had bumped it. Maybe the clock was new but poorly calibrated. Maybe I was tired. All those reasonable possibilities stood between me and the uncomfortable truth that formed in my chest: sometimes time behaves like it has an attitude.

After that, the world seemed to offer more evidence. Not all at once, like a revelation. More like drops of water finding cracks. I would look at my phone after leaving a store and notice I’d lost five minutes without remembering where they went. I would sit in a waiting room and feel sure that an hour had passed, only to see that I’d been there for seventeen. When I drove home, I’d glance at the speedometer and feel the road’s stretch lengthen or shrink depending on how late I thought I was. Time, I realized, wasn’t just something we experienced; it was something we negotiated.

People talk about time the way they talk about weather. There are forecasts, excuses, and resentments. “I’m running out of time,” we say, as if time is a finite resource hidden in a pantry. “I can’t make it—something came up,” we tell each other, as if the universe is always ready with a replacement plan. But what I began to notice, slowly and then with more urgency, was how often we believe our calendars more than our bodies.

If you tell someone, “We’ll meet at six,” there’s an implicit agreement. We agree that the air around us will be shaped into a particular kind of moment: arrival, conversation, maybe laughter. But the meeting doesn’t live inside the number. It lives inside the feelings that gather there—anticipation, impatience, relief, dread. Those feelings take time differently.

I started testing it in small ways. I would do the same task twice with no other changes except my mood. Once, I cleaned my apartment while listening to music I loved. The hours passed like a train sliding through a station: smooth, almost silent, leaving only the faint smell of movement. Another time, I cleaned while listening to nothing, or while thinking about a conversation I dreaded. The exact same actions—scrubbing the same sink, folding the same towels—took on different textures. The second version felt heavier, as if each item had to be lifted not just physically but emotionally.

That was the first time I began to suspect that my experience of time was less like a clock and more like a weather system. Mood wasn’t merely an overlay; it was a climate. It altered how long things felt, yes, but it also altered what counted as “long.” A minute could become a lifetime when you feared bad news. A whole week could feel like a blink when you were laughing so hard you forgot what you were supposed to worry about.

There is a particular kind of person who believes this is all metaphor. They would say, gently, that time perception is subjective, that psychology explains it, that our brains are complicated. I’m not arguing against them. I’m simply saying: even if time perception is subjective, it still has consequences.

Because while we can’t control the mechanics of clocks, we can control—at least somewhat—what we pay attention to. Paying attention is like turning a dial. When you’re busy, time accelerates. When you’re present, it expands. When you’re avoiding something, it warps. The mind is always doing its own accounting, and it doesn’t always match the public record.

I think about this when I’m waiting in line. You can feel the collective impatience in a place like a supermarket checkout. Everyone pretends they are patient, but their bodies tell the truth: bouncing knees, narrowed eyes, the subtle clenching of hands. We look at the clock in the corner and then look away like we’re embarrassed to be caught measuring ourselves. If the line moves quickly, we experience the waiting as not-waiting. If it doesn’t, we experience the air as thick. The same number of customers can feel like a quick shuffle or an endless parade depending on whether we’re willing to let the moment be what it is.

At first, I thought I could use this knowledge for improvement, like learning the trick to a game. If I was late, I would remind myself to breathe, to notice the present, to stop checking. When I was stuck, I would try to make the seconds less sharp. I learned a few techniques: focus on sensory details, name colors, count breaths, loosen your shoulders. It worked—sometimes. But eventually I realized the goal wasn’t to make time feel better. It was to stop treating the moment as an enemy.

The more I paid attention, the stranger it felt that we spend so much energy trying to escape the present. We say we want to “get to the weekend” like the weekend is a country we can immigrate to if we endure the workweek. We talk about “future plans” as if the future is guaranteed, as if time is a road that will always remain open. We carry our lives like bags we can’t set down, convinced that the correct moment to rest is elsewhere.

And then, quietly, we discover what all people discover eventually: time doesn’t care about our plans. It doesn’t even care about our honesty. It arrives in its own way. It takes people. It changes bodies. It rearranges routines until the old clocks are irrelevant.

The strangest part is how ordinary it all is. There’s no trumpeting when a year passes. No dramatic unveiling. It just accumulates, like dust. One day you realize you’ve been wearing the same kind of shoes for so long that you forgot what the world looked like when you chose them. You realize you’ve said the same phrase to yourself—“I’ll do it soon”—so many times that it has become a lullaby. “Soon” is a soft word that lets you postpone without feeling like a villain.

I began to think about the lying clock again. Maybe it wasn’t lying at all. Maybe it was doing something more honest: reminding me that public time doesn’t necessarily match personal time. Maybe the clock’s jump was simply how it compensated for the moments it couldn’t measure, the seconds it lost to dust and mechanics. Maybe it was a small, blunt metaphor for all our systems—how they keep trying to be accurate even when they can’t fully capture the living thing they claim to represent.

One evening I went back to the library hallway. The clock looked the same: dull metal, stubborn face, hands moving with their practiced confidence. I stood there for a while, not waiting for anyone this time. I watched the way people walked past it, how some glanced up with mild curiosity and others never noticed it at all. I thought about how many seconds were happening right now, everywhere, inside everyone. The clock wasn’t measuring them; it was pointing to the illusion that measurement could be universal.

Then a child walked by with her parent, tugging at their sleeve. She looked at the clock and asked a question in a voice that sounded like it had been invented for the moment: “Is it really that time?” Her parent answered, laughing softly, “Yes, it is.” The child seemed satisfied, and yet her eyes kept returning to the face of the clock the way people return to a thing they sense might not be fully true.

I wanted to tell her something else. Not a correction—no, not that. I wanted to tell her that even if the numbers were accurate, the important part of time wasn’t located on the face. The important part was the feeling of asking, the noticing, the way her curiosity made the moment feel newly made. If she learned anything from that, she would be richer than any person who can recite the hour without feeling the weight of it.

As I turned to leave, I realized that I wasn’t angry at the clock anymore. I wasn’t even disappointed. It had done what it was always doing: it offered a reference point in a world that doesn’t hold still. But I also had my own reference point—my body, my attention, my ability to notice. Those were the things that moved honestly with me.

Outside, the sky was beginning to darken. Streetlights blinked on in a slow, mechanical sequence, like a new set of rules entering the scene. Cars passed. Somewhere a door slammed. Somewhere a laugh rose and fell. Time, in all its variations, kept going—not as a single line but as a many-threaded fabric. And in that fabric, the most important moments weren’t those the clock could measure. They were the ones that made me look up.
